summary: This document defines the pushed authorization request endpoint, where an OAuth 2.0 client sends the payload of an authorization request directly to the authorization server and gets back a request URI. That URI is used as a reference to the data in the later call to the authorization endpoint.

eli5.summary: Rather than shouting your order across the room, you give it to the cashier directly and get a ticket number. Later you only show the number.

questions: what is a pushed authorization request
subtitle: A way for an OAuth client to hand its authorization request straight to the server and get back a short reference to use instead.

tldr.problem: OAuth authorization requests normally travel as URL query parameters through the user's browser, where they can be altered, leaked into logs, or grow too large.
tldr.mechanism: The client POSTs the request parameters directly to a pushed authorization request (PAR) endpoint, authenticating itself, and receives a single-use request_uri that it sends through the browser in place of the parameters.
tldr.outcome: The request is integrity-protected and confidential, the client is authenticated before any user interaction, and the authorization server can reject bad requests early.

today: RFC 9126 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, so it remains the definition of PAR.

sections.title: Why Authorization Requests Needed a Fix
sections.content:
In plain OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749), the client sends authorization request parameters as URI query parameters, redirected through the user agent (the browser). The RFC lists three problems with that approach.

  • There is no cryptographic integrity or authenticity protection, so an attacker could, for example, change the requested scope.
  • There is no confidentiality. The data passes through the user agent in the clear and can leak into web server logs and to other sites through the referrer.
  • URLs can get large, especially with fine-grained authorization data, which can cause processing errors.

JWT-Secured Authorization Request (JAR, RFC 9101) addresses these with signed Request Objects and a request_uri reference. PAR complements JAR by giving clients an interoperable way to push the payload to the server in exchange for a request_uri.

Sending the request with HTTP POST through the browser is not a good substitute: it is optional in RFC 6749 and prohibitively difficult for installed mobile apps, whose browser launches are constrained to GET.
sections.eli5: Normally you write your whole order on a note and pass it from hand to hand, where anyone can read or change it. PAR lets you hand it straight to the person who needs it.

sections.title: The PAR Endpoint and Request
sections.content:
The pushed authorization request endpoint is an HTTP API at the authorization server. It accepts POST requests with application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies (UTF-8), and its URL MUST use https.

The client sends the same parameters it would put in an authorization request, such as client_id, response_type, redirect_uri, scope, state, code_challenge and code_challenge_method. Extensions like PKCE, Resource Indicators and OpenID Connect apply too. The one exception is request_uri, which MUST NOT be provided. The client also authenticates the way it would at the token endpoint.

The server MUST authenticate the client, reject the request if request_uri is present, and validate the request as it would at the authorization endpoint, for example checking the redirect URI and scope. It MAY skip checks it cannot perform yet, but then MUST perform them later at the authorization endpoint.

When JWT client assertion authentication is used, the server's issuer identifier SHOULD be the audience value, and the server MUST accept its issuer identifier, token endpoint URL or PAR endpoint URL as identifying it.
sections.eli5: You walk up to the counter, show your ID, and say your whole order. The cashier checks that you are allowed to order it.

sections.title: Responses and the Authorization Request
sections.content:
On success the server MUST answer with HTTP status 201 and a JSON body with two members. request_uri is a single-use reference to the stored request. expires_in is its lifetime in seconds, at the server's discretion but typically short (the RFC suggests between 5 and 600 seconds).

The request_uri MUST contain a part generated with a cryptographically strong pseudorandom algorithm so it cannot be guessed, and it MUST be bound to the client that posted the request. The server MAY use the form urn:ietf:params:oauth:request_uri:<reference-value>.

Errors use the token endpoint format, with invalid_request as the default code. The endpoint may also return 405 for a non-POST method, 413 if the request is too large, and 429 if the client sends too many requests.

The client then sends the user's browser to the authorization endpoint with just client_id and request_uri. The client MUST use a request_uri only once; servers SHOULD treat it as one-time use but MAY tolerate a browser reload. An expired request_uri MUST be rejected.
sections.eli5: The cashier gives you a ticket number that works once and runs out soon. You show the ticket, not the whole order again.

sections.title: Signed Requests and Redirect URIs
sections.content:
A client MAY push a signed Request Object using the request parameter from JAR. Only the parameters needed for client authentication may appear in the form body next to request. Everything about the authorization request itself MUST be claims inside the JWT. The server decrypts the object if needed, validates the signature, and, if the client has credentials, rejects the request when the authenticated client_id does not match the client_id claim.

PAR also allows relaxing exact matching of redirect URIs. Because the server authenticates the client before the authorization process starts, it MAY let such clients supply redirect_uri values that were not registered in advance, perhaps requiring a certain prefix or letting only a query parameter vary.

This is optional. The server decides what restrictions to apply to supplied redirect URIs.
sections.eli5: If you want to prove the order really came from you, you can sign it. And because the cashier knows who you are, you can say which door to deliver it to, within the rules.

sections.title: Metadata for Requiring PAR
sections.content:
Authorization server metadata (RFC 8414) gains two parameters. pushed_authorization_request_endpoint is the endpoint URL; its presence is enough for a client to know it may use PAR. require_pushed_authorization_requests is a boolean saying the server accepts authorization request data only through PAR; the default is false.

Client metadata (RFC 7591) gains require_pushed_authorization_requests too, saying the client may initiate authorization requests only with PAR; again the default is false.

When PAR is required, the server refuses any authorization endpoint request lacking a request_uri obtained from the PAR endpoint, using the invalid_request error code.
sections.eli5: A shop can put up a sign saying: orders only at the counter, please. Metadata is that sign.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC lists five attacks and their mitigations.

  • Guessing: an attacker may try to guess a valid request_uri, so servers must follow the entropy guidance in JAR.
  • Open redirection: servers MUST accept new redirect URIs only from authenticated clients.
  • Replay: servers SHOULD make request URIs one-time use.
  • Client policy change: policy may change between pushing and use, so servers should check the request against current policy at authorization time.
  • Swapping: an attacker could substitute one request URI for another. Clients SHOULD use PKCE, a unique state or the OIDC nonce parameter.

On privacy, PAR may reduce inadvertent disclosure because request data goes over a secure connection in a message body rather than in a URL passing through the browser in the clear.
sections.eli5: Tickets must be hard to guess, work only once, and be tied to the person who ordered, so nobody can steal or swap them.
